title.en: Optoelectronic junction devices: LED, photodiode and solar cell

heading.en: Diodes that shine and diodes that see

hook.en: The torch in a phone, the sensor that switches on street lights at dusk, and the panels on a rooftop are all p-n junctions. They turn electricity into light, or light into electricity.

objectives.en: Explain how an LED, a photodiode and a solar cell work
Relate the band gap to the colour of an LED
Read the I–V curve of a solar cell

narration.en: The torch in a phone, the sensor that switches on street lights at dusk, and the panels on a rooftop are all p-n junctions. They turn electricity into light, or light into electricity.

body.en: In an LED, a forward-biased junction of a direct band gap semiconductor (such as GaAsP) lets electrons and holes recombine and emit photons of energy close to the band gap: $\lambda \approx hc/E_g$. A photodiode is reverse biased; light of energy above $E_g$ creates electron–hole pairs near the junction, and the reverse current rises in proportion to the light intensity. A solar cell is an unbiased junction with a large area: the junction field separates the pairs made by sunlight and drives a current through a load, giving an emf of about 0.5–0.6 V for silicon.

points.en: Solar cell: no bias, generates an emf

title.en: The I–V curve of a solar cell

narration.en: Change the sunlight. The short-circuit current grows in proportion to the light; the open-circuit voltage grows only slowly. Move the operating point to make the orange rectangle as big as you can.

caption.en: Set the sunlight and the operating voltage (chosen by the load). The yellow curve is the cell's I–V curve in the fourth-quadrant form drawn upright; the orange rectangle's area is the power delivered.

problem.en: A photodiode is made of a semiconductor with a band gap of 2.8 eV. Can it detect light of wavelength 600 nm?

steps.en: 2.07 eV < 2.8 eV, so the photons cannot create electron–hole pairs.

answer.en: No: it detects only λ below about 1240/2.8 ≈ 443 nm

At full sunlight, find the operating voltage that gives the solar cell its greatest power.

prompt.en: At full sunlight (1000 W/m²), choose the operating voltage at which the solar cell delivers the most power. The power is hidden: reason from the curve, then lock in.

explanation.en: The power V × I is greatest at the knee of the curve, about 0.38 V, where it is about 10.5 mW.

hint.en: Near the open-circuit voltage the current collapses; at low voltage the power is small. Look for the knee.

body.en: Light out (LED): forward. Light measured (photodiode): reverse. Light to power (solar cell): no bias at all. Colour from the gap: λ(nm) = 1240/E_g(eV).

points.en: LED: forward bias; photons of energy ≈ E_g, λ ≈ 1240/E_g nm.
Photodiode: reverse bias; the photocurrent is proportional to intensity.
Solar cell: unbiased junction; the junction field separates light-made pairs and gives an emf; best power at the knee of its I–V curve.
